claim: Characterizing the full range of spatial frequencies in scalp EEG (spherical-harmonic degree up to ~7 on a ~9 cm-radius head) requires a minimum of 128 sensors, with 32 or fewer channels described as a sparse montage.

source.authors: Srinivasan R, Tucker DM, Murias M
source.title: Estimating the spatial Nyquist of the human EEG

quote: requires a minimum of 128 sensors
notes: Four-concentric-sphere head model, radius ~9 cm, skull assumed 80x less conductive than brain. Authors also say 'additional increases in sensor density beyond 128 channels will improve the spatial resolution' and that 256-channel studies are needed.

claim: The highest spherical-harmonic degree resolvable without aliasing by common montages is about degree 3 for 19 channels, 4 for 32, 6 for 64 and 7 for 128 channels; degree 9 is visibly distorted even with 128 channels.

source.authors: Srinivasan R, Tucker DM, Murias M
source.title: Estimating the spatial Nyquist of the human EEG

evidence_location: Body (simulation results); wavenumber k=(n+1)/R with R~9 cm
quote: (no verbatim sentence captured; extraction paraphrased the body text)
notes: Numbers were read from the full-text PDF by the extraction step but reported as paraphrase, not verbatim; re-check figures before quoting exact degrees. Same source also states the smallest feature accurately resolved by a 32-channel array is ~7 cm in diameter.

claim: Nearest-neighbour inter-electrode spacing on a geodesic layout is just under 5 cm for 32 sensors, just under 4 cm for 64 and just under 3 cm for 128, versus roughly 7 cm for the 19-channel Ten-Twenty system.

source.authors: Srinivasan R, Tucker DM, Murias M
source.title: Estimating the spatial Nyquist of the human EEG

evidence_location: Body (Introduction/Methods, discussion of Spitzer et al. 1989 and geodesic sensor nets)
quote: (paraphrased by extraction; verbatim sentence not captured)
notes: Engineering Nyquist criterion used: sample at >2.5x the highest spatial frequency rather than 2x.

claim: Using a 64-channel linear scalp array with 3 mm inter-electrode spacing in 9 awake humans, spatial power spectra of scalp EEG showed peaks especially at 0.1-0.4 cycles/cm (wavelengths ~2.5-10 cm), and the authors concluded optimal scalp electrode spacing might be about 1 cm.

source.authors: Freeman WJ, Holmes MD, Burke BC, Vanhatalo S
source.title: Spatial spectra of scalp EEG and EMG from awake humans

quote: especially 0.1-0.4 cycles/cm
notes: Range field holds the spatial-spectral peak band in cycles/cm. Abstract attributes the spatial distortion (steeper, non-linear fall-off vs. intracranial 1/f) mainly to smearing by dura, skull and scalp. DOI supplied from memory.

claim: A finite-element simulation by the Freeman group argued that the practical spatial Nyquist for scalp EEG should be 3.0 cycles/cm, implying an optimal inter-electrode spacing of about 3 mm to extract gyral-scale cortical patterns.

source.authors: Ramon C, Freeman WJ, Holmes MD, Ishimaru A, Haueisen J, Schimpf PH, Rezvanian E
source.title: Similarities between simulated spatial spectra of scalp EEG, MEG and structural MRI

quote: the practical Nyquist frequency for sampling scalp EEGs should be 3.0 cycles/cm
notes: Simulation-only (2 x 2 x 3.2 mm FEM voxels), a minority view that conflicts with the ~1-3 cm estimates of Srinivasan 1998 and Iivanainen et al.; useful as the optimistic bound. Title and DOI supplied from memory (the fetched PDF confirmed authors, journal, volume and pages only).

claim: In a three-layer spherical head model with singular-value-decomposition analysis, dense arrays up to 256 electrodes (16 mm spacing) improved inverse cortical-potential estimates only with low realistic noise; as noise increases the advantage of dense systems decreases, but at least 64 electrodes is always beneficial in clinical environments.

source.authors: Ryynänen ORM, Hyttinen JAK, Laarne PH, Malmivuo JA
source.title: Effect of electrode density and measurement noise on the spatial resolution of cortical potential distribution

quote: it is always beneficial to have at least 64 measurement electrodes
notes: Abstract seen on a mirror; no numeric noise levels or skull resistivities in the abstract. The companion 2006 paper (IEEE TBME 53:1851, with realistic skull conductivity) was not opened.

claim: With interictal spikes recorded from 123 electrodes in 14 epilepsy patients, the EEG source was significantly closer to the lesion with 63 than with 31 electrodes in 9/14 patients, and going to 123 electrodes raised this to 11/14.

source.authors: Lantz G, Grave de Peralta R, Spinelli L, Seeck M, Michel CM
source.title: Epileptic source localization with high density EEG: how many electrodes are needed?

quote: increasing the number of electrodes to 123 increased this number of patients from 9 to 11
notes: A 2018 review (Mégevand & Seeck, Curr Opin Neurol) summarises this as 'the largest increment in accuracy occurred when the number of electrodes increased from 31 to 63'. DOI from memory.

claim: Generalized spatial-frequency analysis of a realistic four-compartment head model found that about 110 spatial-frequency components capture 99% of the scalp-EEG topography energy of the most superficial sources (versus ~300 for on-scalp MEG), corresponding to a 99% bandwidth of ~120 1/m and a required EEG sensor spacing of ~2.6 cm, i.e. roughly 120 sensors for an adult head.

source.authors: Iivanainen J, Mäkinen AJ, Zetter R, Stenroos M, Ilmoniemi RJ, Parkkonen L
source.title: Spatial sampling of MEG and EEG based on generalized spatial-frequency analysis and optimal design
source.journal: NeuroImage (preprint: arXiv:1912.05401, 'Sampling theory for spatial field sensing: Application to electro- and magnetoencephalography')

quote: approximately 300, 100 and 110 SF components were needed in on-scalp, off-scalp MEG and EEG, respectively
notes: Verified in the arXiv full text; the journal version details (NeuroImage 245:118747, DOI) are from memory. Skull conductivity 0.33/50 S/m. In a single-compartment (no skull) model the count rises to 300-350, showing the skull removes the high-spatial-frequency energy: 'the topography energy is reduced in EEG from 1C to 4C'.

claim: For independent, identically distributed cortical sources in a realistic head model, only 25 eigencomponents are needed to explain 99% of the variance of scalp EEG (maximum 62 across source sets), versus 88 for on-scalp MEG and 35 for conventional MEG.

source.authors: Iivanainen J, Mäkinen AJ, Zetter R, Stenroos M, Ilmoniemi RJ, Parkkonen L
source.title: Spatial sampling of MEG and EEG based on generalized spatial-frequency analysis and optimal design

quote: 88, 35 and 25 eigencomponents are needed in on-scalp MEG, off-scalp MEG and EEG
notes: This is the closest published analogue to an 'effective number of independent channels' of scalp EEG for distributed cortical activity.

claim: With noise included, about 20 EEG samples (sensors) suffice to explain 90% of the variance of IID cortical sources at low noise, whereas at high noise even 400 EEG samples explain only 80% of the variance; for a small motor-cortex region of interest only 8 EEG components had signal-to-noise ratio above 1.
units: components with SNR > 1 (motor-cortex ROI, white noise)

source.authors: Iivanainen J, Mäkinen AJ, Zetter R, Stenroos M, Ilmoniemi RJ, Parkkonen L
source.title: Spatial sampling of MEG and EEG based on generalized spatial-frequency analysis and optimal design

quote: Nine and eight components had SNR > 1 in on-scalp MEG and EEG when white noise was considered.
notes: The 8-component figure applies to a localized motor-cortex ROI, not whole-brain EEG. Supporting quotes: 'about 80, 30 and 20 samples are needed to explain 90% variance' (low noise) and 'only 60%, 74% and 80% of variance is explained' (high noise), order on-scalp MEG, off-scalp MEG, EEG.

claim: Decomposing 71-channel EEG from 13 subjects, the best ICA algorithm (AMICA) yielded on average only 34 of 71 components (48%) whose scalp maps were near-dipolar (residual variance < 10%), Infomax about 42%, and PCA only 3 of 71.

source.authors: Delorme A, Palmer J, Onton J, Oostenveld R, Makeig S
source.title: Independent EEG sources are dipolar

evidence_location: Results text and Table 1 (dipolarity at 10% residual-variance threshold)
quote: on average 34/71 or 48%
notes: 71 channels = 69 scalp + 2 periocular; 14 subjects recorded, 1 excluded. Dipolarity correlated with mutual-information reduction (r^2 = 0.96). Dipole fits used a spherical head model. Note the near-dipolar set includes non-brain (eye, muscle) components, so the count of independent brain sources is lower still.

claim: The EEG inverse problem is ill-posed: the number of candidate source parameters p is far larger than the number of electrodes N (p >> N), making it underdetermined, with scalp electrode counts described as usually fewer than 100.

source.authors: Grech R, Cassar T, Muscat J, Camilleri KP, Fabri SG, Zervakis M, Xanthopoulos P, Sakkalis V, Vanrumste B
source.title: Review on solving the inverse problem in EEG source analysis

quote: yielding large p >> N which makes the problem underdetermined
notes: Helmholtz (1853) and 'silent'/closed-field sources are NOT mentioned in this review; cite Michel et al. 2004 or Nunez & Srinivasan 2006 for those (not opened here).

claim: Mammalian cortical networks show oscillatory bands spanning roughly 0.05 Hz to 500 Hz, and the oscillation period is constrained by the size of the neuronal pool engaged in each cycle, with very large networks recruited during slow oscillations.

source.authors: Buzsáki G, Draguhn A
source.title: Neuronal oscillations in cortical networks

evidence_location: p. 1926, section 'A System of Brain Oscillators'
quote: the period of oscillation is constrained by the size of the neuronal pool engaged in a given cycle
notes: The paper does not explicitly state that scalp EEG requires population synchrony; it describes waking scalp EEG as low-amplitude 'desynchronized' patterns. For the explicit synchrony requirement use Nunez & Srinivasan 2006 (not opened).

claim: The adult male human brain contains on average 86.1 +/- 8.1 billion neurons, of which only 19% (about 16 billion) are in the cerebral cortex.

source.authors: Azevedo FAC, Carvalho LRB, Grinberg LT, Farfel JM, Ferretti REL, Leite REP, Jacob Filho W, Lent R, Herculano-Houzel S
source.title: Equal numbers of neuronal and nonneuronal cells make the human brain an isometrically scaled-up primate brain

quote: the adult male human brain contains on average 86.1 +/- 8.1 billion NeuN-positive cells
notes: Abstract gives the cortical share as a percentage ('With only 19% of all neurons located in the cerebral cortex'); 0.19 x 86.1e9 = 16.4e9 is a derived figure. Range field is mean +/- 1 SD.

claim: As of 2002, the best brain-computer interfaces (essentially all EEG-based) had maximum information transfer rates of only 10-25 bits per minute.

source.authors: Wolpaw JR, Birbaumer N, McFarland DJ, Pfurtscheller G, Vaughan TM
source.title: Brain-computer interfaces for communication and control

quote: Current BCIs have maximum information transfer rates up to 10-25 bits/min.
notes: Section 4 adds 'Present independent BCIs in their best moments reach 25 bits/min.'

claim: A 40-character steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) speller using 0.5-s joint frequency-phase coded flicker reached information transfer rates up to 5.32 bits per second (about 319 bits/min), the highest reported for any BCI speller at the time.

source.authors: Chen X, Wang Y, Nakanishi M, Gao X, Jung T-P, Gao S
source.title: High-speed spelling with a noninvasive brain-computer interface
source.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA

quote: information transfer rates (ITRs) up to 5.32 bits per second
notes: Abstract seen on a PubMed mirror (PMC blocked by CAPTCHA). Note SSVEP spellers exploit stimulus-driven visual responses, not volitional dimensionality; the user chooses among 40 externally flickered targets.

claim: A 40-target SSVEP speller with task-related component analysis achieved online information transfer rates averaging 325.33 +/- 38.17 bits/min in a cue-guided task (20 subjects) and 198.67 +/- 50.48 bits/min in free spelling (10 subjects).

source.authors: Nakanishi M, Wang Y, Chen X, Wang Y-T, Gao X, Jung T-P
source.title: Enhancing detection of SSVEPs for a high-speed brain speller using task-related component analysis

quote: achieved averaged information transfer rates (ITRs) of 325.33 +/- 38.17 bits/min with the cue-guided task
notes: 325 bits/min = 5.4 bits/s; still the ballpark ceiling for non-invasive EEG. DOI from memory.

claim: Humans, including people with spinal cord injury, learned to control a two-dimensional cursor movement signal from scalp EEG sensorimotor rhythms, with movement time, precision and accuracy reported as comparable to invasive BCIs in monkeys.

source.authors: Wolpaw JR, McFarland DJ
source.title: Control of a two-dimensional movement signal by a noninvasive brain-computer interface in humans
source.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA

quote: In movement time, precision, and accuracy, the results are comparable to those with invasive BCIs.
notes: Abstract seen on the Wadsworth/NCAN bibliography page; number of subjects (4) and mu/beta band details are in the full text, which was not opened. DOI from memory.

claim: Four adults learned simultaneous control of three independent EEG signals (one per dimension) from 3-Hz-wide sensorimotor-rhythm bands (centre frequencies 10-31 Hz) at 3-4 electrodes, reaching targets in a virtual cube in 93%, 78%, 76% and 56% of trials.

source.authors: McFarland DJ, Sarnacki WA, Wolpaw JR
source.title: Electroencephalographic (EEG) control of three-dimensional movement

quote: People acquire simultaneous control of three independent signals (one for each dimension).
notes: Range field = percent of trials in which target was reached in time. EEG recorded from 64 scalp locations but control features came from 3-4 electrodes (e.g., Cz, CPz, C3, C4). Three dimensions is the most independent volitional continuous control signals verified here for scalp EEG.

claim: Linear-regression reconstruction of limb kinematics from low-frequency scalp EEG produced positive correlations that a systematic statistical analysis showed were not above chance level, where chance was estimated by randomly pairing recorded velocity profiles with EEG.

source.authors: Antelis JM, Montesano L, Ramos-Murguialday A, Birbaumer N, Minguez J
source.title: On the usage of linear regression models to reconstruct limb kinematics from low frequency EEG signals

quote: these results were not above the chance level
notes: Directly challenges Bradberry, Gentili & Contreras-Vidal 2010 (J Neurosci 30:3432), which was NOT opened here; its correlation values (~0.2-0.4) are not verified. Antelis also notes correlation 'is invariant to scale', which 'could lead to overly-optimistic results'.

claim: An intracortical handwriting BCI (two 96-channel arrays in motor cortex, one participant with spinal cord injury) achieved 90 characters per minute with 94.1% raw online accuracy and >99% offline with autocorrect, exceeding any other BCI.

source.authors: Willett FR, Avansino DT, Hochberg LR, Henderson JM, Shenoy KV
source.title: High-performance brain-to-text communication via handwriting

quote: achieved typing speeds of 90 characters per minute with 94.1% raw accuracy online
notes: The abstract does not state the array count; 'two 96-channel arrays' is from memory of the Methods and should be checked. Abstract also notes smartphone typing for the participant's age group is ~115 characters/min.

claim: An intracortical speech BCI using four microelectrode arrays decoded attempted speech at 62 words per minute, 3.4 times the previous BCI record (18 words/min for the handwriting BCI), with 9.1% word error rate on a 50-word vocabulary and 23.8% on a 125,000-word vocabulary.

source.authors: Willett FR, Kunz EM, Fan C, Avansino DT, Wilson GH, Choi EY, Kamdar F, Glasser MF, Hochberg LR, Druckmann S, Jaffe LA, Shenoy KV, Henderson JM
source.title: A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis

evidence_location: Abstract; main text (array count and prior record)
quote: decoded at 62 words per minute, which is 3.4 times as fast as the previous record
notes: Main text: 'we recorded neural activity from four microelectrode arrays' and 'the previous state of the art for any type of BCI (18 words per minute for a handwriting BCI)'. Natural conversation is ~160 words/min.

claim: Three people with paralysis using intracortical BCIs achieved mean copy-typing rates of 13.5-39.2 correct characters per minute and achieved bitrates of 1.4-4.2 bits/s on a grid task (best block 4.36 bits/s), exceeding prior intracortical BCIs by 1.4-4.2x in typing rate and 2.2-4.0x in throughput.

source.authors: Pandarinath C, Nuyujukian P, Blabe CH, Sorice BL, Saab J, Willett FR, Hochberg LR, Shenoy KV, Henderson JM
source.title: High performance communication by people with paralysis using an intracortical brain-computer interface

evidence_location: Abstract (improvement factors); Table 1 and figure/video captions (absolute values)
quote: information throughput (by a factor of 2.2-4.0)
notes: Per-participant means: T6 2.2 +/- 0.4 bps, T5 3.7 +/- 0.4 (6x6) and 4.16 +/- 0.39 (9x9), T7 1.4 +/- 0.1 bps; three-participant average 28.1 ccpm and 2.4 bps. Compare the EEG SSVEP ceiling of ~5.3 bits/s (t6-16/17), which however relies on externally driven visual stimuli rather than volitional control.
